messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar, a 40-year-old Middle Eastern software engineer, had been living in Houston with his wife when the storm hit their neighborhood with a violence that felt unreal even to him now. He had gone to the apartment complex garage to move the car after the first reports of flooding, and within minutes the water was up around his legs, rising fast and carrying debris, while somewhere nearby an alarm shrieked and an ambulance siren cut in and out through the rain. He remembered the sound of metal grinding against concrete, the panic in people’s voices, and the shock of cold water pulling at him as he tried to reach higher ground. In the weeks that followed, he found that the memory would come back with startling force: sometimes the scene returned in pieces and he could not put the order together correctly, and sometimes it landed all at once, fully sensory, as though he were back in the garage with the same water, the same noise, and the same helpless urgency. When that happened, he would even hear fragments of the sounds from that night in his head, vivid enough to make him grip the edge of a desk or stop walking until it passed.

Omar had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and he carried that comparison with a harsh sense of personal failure. He told himself that nothing good could happen to him anymore and that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable. Those appraisals made every reminder feel dangerous: if the world could turn that suddenly against him once, then it could do so again at any time. He became jumpy at unexpected movement nearby, reacting as if he were in immediate danger when a colleague stood up quickly beside his cubicle or when his wife came up behind him and touched his shoulder without warning. In the office, where he spent long hours writing code, he found himself checking the hallway and stairwells before he could settle at his desk, and in restaurants or parking garages he always identified the escape routes before he felt comfortable enough to sit down. The more he was overtaken by the memory of the flood, the more his body seemed to live in that same emergency, and the more certain he became that he had to scan for danger because the memory itself proved how quickly things could turn.

As these episodes repeated, Omar tried to manage them by forcing himself to think only positive thoughts and by pushing away anything that reminded him of hospitals, ambulances, or physical examinations. He told himself that if he stayed upbeat and refused to dwell on the disaster, he could keep the fear under control. But the effort left him more tense and vigilant, and the very act of suppressing what had happened made the memories break through more sharply and with less warning. When they did, they carried the threat with them: the sounds in his head, the sense that it was happening again, and the certainty that he was never really safe. That heightened alarm fed back into his thinking, and after another night of reliving the garage scene he would be left even more convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore. He noticed that he was no longer the happy person he used to be, and each failed attempt to stay positive seemed to confirm that loss.

His alarm also pushed him toward other habits that kept the fear alive. He ruminated about how to get even with the “assailant,” a word he used for the storm and the sudden force that had trapped him, imagining in a grim, repetitive way how he might have acted differently or how he would not be caught helpless again. Those thoughts did not bring relief; they left him more keyed up, more watchful, and more ready to flinch at touch or movement. Even at home he would start if his wife came into the kitchen too quickly or if the doorbell rang unexpectedly, and he hated how exposed he felt in places without a clear exit. The loop had narrowed his world. He had begun avoiding medical settings altogether, turning down a recommended checkup after a minor chest tightness episode because the waiting room, the smell of disinfectant, and the idea of being examined felt too close to the storm’s helplessness. Over time, that avoidance, the constant scanning, and the grim private rehearsals of revenge left him more isolated from his wife and more strained at work, where he feared appearing distracted or weak. What finally brought him to seek help was realizing that the memories were becoming more intrusive and more vivid, and that his life was shrinking around them. He hoped to stop feeling as though danger were always about to arrive, but he was most afraid that if he let his guard down even briefly, the flood and everything it had taken from him would come rushing back.
